cards.front: Name the two cyclooxygenase isoforms and the role of each.
cards.back: COX-1 is constitutive and maintains housekeeping functions such as gastric mucosal protection and platelet TXA2. COX-2 is induced by cytokines at inflamed sites and drives local prostaglandin generation. COX-2 is also present constitutively in brain, juxtaglomerular cells and the foetus.

cards.front: How does aspirin inhibit COX differently from most other NSAIDs?
cards.back: Aspirin acetylates a serine residue of COX irreversibly, so activity returns only when new enzyme is synthesised. Most other NSAIDs are competitive and reversible; their effect ends when the drug dissociates from the enzyme.

cards.front: Why does a low daily dose of aspirin protect platelets for about a week, while ibuprofen's antiplatelet effect is short?
cards.back: Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX-1 and hence TXA2 synthesis. Platelets cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts about a week, the platelet lifespan. Ibuprofen binds reversibly and its effect is short lived.

cards.front: Why is paracetamol a good antipyretic but a poor anti-inflammatory drug?
cards.back: It is a weak inhibitor of peripheral COX. Peroxides generated at inflamed sites block its action there, but no such peroxides are present in the brain, where it inhibits COX well. Action on the brain isoform COX-3 may also contribute.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of paracetamol-induced hepatic injury?
cards.back: A minor oxidative metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NABQI), is normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. After a very large dose, glucuronidation saturates, more NABQI forms and hepatic glutathione is depleted. NABQI then binds liver and renal tubular proteins, causing necrosis.

cards.front: What paracetamol dose signals serious toxicity, and when is fatality likely?
cards.back: KDT: above about 150 mg/kg (over 10 g in an adult) can cause serious toxicity, and fatality is common above about 250 mg/kg. GG14: hepatotoxicity may follow a single 10 to 15 g (150 to 250 mg/kg) in adults or more than 150 mg/kg in children; 20 to 25 g or more is potentially fatal. Alcoholics and fasting or malnourished patients are at risk at lower doses. Early features are only nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain; centrilobular necrosis develops after 12 to 18 hours, clinical liver damage shows in 2 to 4 days, and transaminases peak at 72 to 96 hours.

cards.front: Paracetamol poisoning: antidote, how it works, and the dosing regimen.
cards.back: N-acetylcysteine (NAC). It replenishes hepatic glutathione and can also conjugate NAPQI directly, so the toxic metabolite is detoxified instead of binding liver proteins. Standard regimen (GG12): IV 150 mg/kg over 60 min, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h; or oral 140 mg/kg loading, then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 17 doses. KDT gives a simpler scheme: 150 mg/kg IV over 15 min, then the same dose over 20 h, or 75 mg/kg orally every 4 to 6 h for 2 to 3 days. Start before blood levels return if overdose is suspected; given within 8 to 16 h, mortality falls below 1%, but it is practically ineffective if started 16 h or later. Side effects: rash, nausea, vomiting, rare anaphylactoid reactions.

cards.front: Which analgesic-antipyretic is safest in pregnancy, and why is aspirin avoided in children with viral infections?
cards.back: Paracetamol is the safest choice in pregnancy, with low-dose aspirin probably second best. Aspirin is avoided in children with varicella or influenza because of its link with Reye's syndrome, a rare hepatic encephalopathy; paediatric aspirin formulations are prohibited in India and the UK.

cards.front: List the main mechanisms of NSAID-induced gastric mucosal injury.
cards.back: Loss of COX-1-derived protective PGE2 and PGI2 reduces mucus and bicarbonate secretion, increases acid secretion and reduces mucosal blood flow. Back-diffusion of H+ ions in the mucosa adds to the damage. Misoprostol, a stable PG analogue, counteracts NSAID gastric toxicity.

cards.front: What happens when ibuprofen is taken with low-dose aspirin?
cards.back: Ibuprofen occupies the active site of platelet COX-1 reversibly, so aspirin cannot acetylate it. This abolishes aspirin's antiplatelet and cardioprotective effect, so ibuprofen should not be used in patients relying on aspirin for cardioprotection.

cards.front: Why were rofecoxib and valdecoxib withdrawn?
cards.back: Both were linked to increased myocardial infarction. Rofecoxib was stopped in the APPROVE trial and withdrawn globally in 2004; valdecoxib was withdrawn in 2005 after cardiac events in patients undergoing bypass surgery, and also because of severe skin reactions.

cards.front: What are the main safety concerns with nimesulide, and where is it still specifically useful?
cards.back: It can cause fulminant hepatic failure and has been withdrawn in several countries; its use in children is banned in India. Its specific value lies in patients with asthma or aspirin intolerance, most of whom do not cross-react with it.

cards.front: Classify: NSAIDs by chemical class

cards.front: Classify: selective COX-2 inhibitors
cards.text: Among the coxibs, {{etoricoxib}} has the highest COX-2 selectivity and is given once daily; {{celecoxib}} is metabolised mainly by {{CYP2C9}}; {{parecoxib}} is an injectable prodrug of {{valdecoxib}}.

cards.front: Classify: key facts about aspirin
cards.text: Aspirin is converted to {{salicylic acid}}; its antiplatelet effect results from {{irreversible}} acetylation of COX-1 and lasts about {{one week}}; low-dose secondary prevention uses {{75 to 150 mg}} daily; analgesic doses are {{0.3 to 0.6 g}} every 6 to 8 hours.

cards.front: Classify: NSAID adverse effects by system
cards.text: Renal: {{sodium and water retention}} and {{papillary necrosis}}; hepatic: {{raised transaminases}}; CNS: {{tinnitus}} and {{confusion}}; haematological: {{thrombocytopenia}} and {{haemolytic anaemia}}; respiratory: {{asthma}} in aspirin-sensitive patients.

cards.front: Classify: drugs used to close a patent ductus arteriosus
cards.text: Ductus arteriosus is kept open by {{PGE2}} made by {{COX-2}}; after birth it closes naturally, but if it does not, small doses of {{indomethacin}} or {{aspirin}} close it by blocking PG synthesis.

cards.front: What is a DMARD, and how does it differ from an NSAID?
cards.back: A disease-modifying antirheumatic drug suppresses the rheumatoid process and slows progression. Unlike NSAIDs it has no nonspecific anti-inflammatory or analgesic action. Benefit takes months to appear, and relapse occurs after stopping.

cards.front: Why is methotrexate the first-choice DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis, and how does it act?
cards.back: It is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor that reduces proliferation of immune-inflammatory cells and cytokine production. Relief starts in 3 to 6 weeks, response is predictable and sustained, and the weekly oral low dose (7.5 to 15 mg) is well accepted. It is standard even in juvenile RA.

cards.front: What are the serious toxicities of methotrexate, and when is it contraindicated?
cards.back: Oral ulceration and GI upset are common. Prolonged use causes dose-related liver damage progressing to cirrhosis, and chest infections increase. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, breast-feeding, liver disease, active infection, leucopenia and peptic ulcer, and is avoided in renal disease because excretion is impaired.

cards.front: Which drugs increase methotrexate levels or toxicity?
cards.back: Aspirin and probenecid raise methotrexate levels by reducing its excretion. Trimethoprim adds to dihydrofolate reductase inhibition and can depress bone marrow.

cards.front: What is sulfasalazine made of, and what is its role in RA?
cards.back: It is sulfapyridine linked to 5-aminosalicylic acid. In RA it is a second-line or add-on DMARD of modest efficacy. Neutropenia or thrombocytopenia occurs in about 5 to 10% of patients, so blood counts need monitoring.

cards.front: Why is hydroxychloroquine preferred over chloroquine when used in RA?
cards.back: Both take 3 to 6 months to act and do not prevent bony erosions. Retinal damage and corneal opacity are the main concern; these are less frequent and reversible with hydroxychloroquine. It is best reserved for mild, non-erosive disease.

cards.front: How does leflunomide act, and why is a loading dose needed?
cards.back: It is converted to an active metabolite that inhibits dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase, blocking pyrimidine synthesis in dividing cells. The metabolite has a half-life of 2 to 3 weeks, so a loading dose of 100 mg daily for 3 days precedes 20 mg daily. It must not be used in pregnancy or children.

cards.front: What is the main use of azathioprine in RA, and what interaction limits its dose?
cards.back: It is converted to 6-mercaptopurine and is used mainly for its steroid-sparing effect, especially in systemic disease. It is not combined with methotrexate. Allopurinol inhibits its breakdown, so the azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine dose is cut to about one-third.

cards.front: How do TNF inhibitors work, and what is their main hazard?
cards.back: They neutralise TNF, either as a soluble receptor or an antibody, reducing macrophage and T-cell activation. They act faster than conventional DMARDs and slow erosions. The main hazard is opportunistic infection, including tuberculosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia, because TNF is needed against granulomatous infection.

cards.front: How does abatacept act, and with which drug must it not be combined?
cards.back: It is a CTLA-4 Fc fusion protein that binds CD80 and CD86, blocking the second costimulatory signal needed for T-cell activation. It is used in active RA not responding to methotrexate. It must not be combined with TNF antagonists because infection risk rises greatly.

cards.front: How does colchicine act in acute gout, and what limits its use?
cards.back: It binds tubulin and so blocks granulocyte migration into the joint and the release of chemotactic factors and glycoprotein. It has no general analgesic or anti-inflammatory effect, and it does not change uric acid levels; its action is specific to gouty inflammation. Dose-related GI toxicity limits it, so it is second line to NSAIDs.

cards.front: What is the role of allopurinol in chronic gout, and what is its mechanism?
cards.back: Its metabolite alloxanthine is a long-acting, noncompetitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid synthesis. It is the first-choice drug for chronic gout, in both over-producers and under-excretors. It must not be started during an acute attack, and NSAID or colchicine cover is needed for 1 to 2 months.

cards.front: JAK inhibitors in rheumatoid arthritis: mechanism, agents and key adverse effects.
cards.back: Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2) are tyrosine kinases activated by cytokine receptors; they phosphorylate STAT transcription factors that switch on inflammatory genes. Oral JAK inhibitors block this signalling and cytokine production. Tofacitinib (JAK1/JAK3, 5 mg twice daily) is used in severe RA not responding to methotrexate, alone or with methotrexate, but not with azathioprine, cyclosporine or biological DMARDs. Other JAK inhibitors approved for RA include baricitinib (JAK1/JAK2) and upadacitinib (JAK1). Adverse effects: respiratory infections, reactivation of tuberculosis, headache, diarrhoea, hypertension, anaemia and liver damage. GG14: a boxed warning covers serious infections, malignancy, thrombosis, major cardiovascular events and death, and since 2021 the US label limits them to patients who respond poorly to TNF antagonists.
